questions.prompt: A spatial join matches records by:
questions.explain: Location takes the place of the key.

questions.prompt: When do you need a spatial join instead of an attribute join?
choices: When the two layers share no key field, only a location
When both tables have a FIPS code
When the tables are sorted differently
When one table is a CSV
questions.explain: EMS calls and neighborhoods share no ID, so location must do the matching.

questions.prompt: A spatial join tool usually writes a new output layer and leaves the input layers unchanged.
questions.explain: Both QGIS and ArcGIS Pro write the result to a new layer.

questions.prompt: An inside join matches features that:
choices: Contain, lie within, or intersect each other
questions.explain: For example, a point inside a polygon.

questions.prompt: A distance join matches each feature to:
choices: The closest feature, or features within a set distance
The feature with the same key
questions.explain: It can also record the distance.

questions.prompt: QGIS calls the rules that decide whether two features match:
questions.explain: ArcGIS Pro calls them match options.

questions.prompt: The intersects predicate is true when two geometries:
questions.explain: It is the most general test.

questions.prompt: The touches predicate is true when two geometries:
choices: Share a boundary but their interiors don't overlap
questions.explain: Two neighboring counties touch.

questions.prompt: Disjoint geometries:
questions.explain: Disjoint is the opposite of intersects.

questions.prompt: For points and polygons, intersects and within differ only for:
choices: Points exactly on a polygon's boundary
questions.explain: Intersects counts a boundary point; within does not.

questions.prompt: Which county is each school in? This is a:
questions.explain: Each school lies in one county.

questions.prompt: How many schools are in each county? This is a:
questions.explain: Each county contains many schools.

questions.prompt: Which attraction is closest to each hotel, and how far? This is a:
questions.explain: Each hotel has one nearest attraction.

questions.prompt: How many attractions are closer to each hotel than to any other hotel? This is a:
questions.explain: Each hotel collects many attractions.

questions.prompt: To count the schools in each county, the destination layer is:
questions.explain: One row of the answer is a county.

questions.prompt: The surest way to choose the destination layer is to ask:
choices: What should one row of the output represent?
questions.explain: That row is a feature of the destination layer.

questions.prompt: A simple spatial join suits which cardinalities?
questions.explain: Each destination feature matches at most one source feature.

questions.prompt: A summarized spatial join is needed when the cardinality is:
questions.explain: Several matches have to be collapsed into statistics.

questions.prompt: Each septic system lies in exactly one geology polygon; many septic systems share a polygon. Joining geology to the septic systems is:
questions.explain: Each septic point gets one rock type.

questions.prompt: Each city has one nearest airport, and many cities can share it. Cities to nearest airport is:
questions.explain: A simple distance join works.

questions.prompt: Every summarized join adds:
choices: A count of the matching features
questions.explain: ArcGIS Pro calls it Join_Count. Sum, mean, min, and max are optional.

questions.prompt: Schools have an enrollment field. To get the number of students in each district, use a summarized join with:
questions.explain: Sum adds up the enrollments of all the schools in each district.

questions.prompt: You run a simple join where each county contains many schools. What happens?
choices: The software keeps one match (usually the first) and drops the rest
questions.explain: That silently loses data. Use a summarized join.

questions.prompt: A distance join on layers stored in WGS84 (EPSG:4326) reports distances in:
questions.explain: Distances come out in the stored units of the data.

questions.prompt: About how long is one degree of latitude, anywhere on Earth?
questions.explain: It varies only slightly, from about 110.6 to 111.7 km.

questions.prompt: About how many kilometers long is one degree of longitude at 45° N?
questions.explain: It shrinks with the cosine of the latitude: about 111 × cos 45° ≈ 79 km.

questions.prompt: Where is a degree of longitude longest?
questions.explain: Meridians converge toward the poles.

questions.prompt: At 45° N, attraction A is 0.9° east of a hotel and B is 0.8° north. Which is closer on the ground?
questions.explain: 0.9 × 79 km ≈ 71 km; 0.8 × 111 km ≈ 89 km. In degrees, B looks closer.

questions.prompt: Setting the map's coordinate system to UTM fixes a distance join on data stored in degrees.
questions.explain: The tools read the stored coordinates. Project the data with Reproject Layer or Project.

questions.prompt: How do you fix a distance join on data stored in a GCS?
choices: Project both layers into a suitable projected CRS, then rerun the join
questions.explain: In QGIS use Reproject Layer; in ArcGIS Pro use Project.

questions.prompt: Which QGIS tool runs a simple distance join?
questions.explain: Set 1 neighbor for the closest feature.

questions.prompt: Which QGIS tool runs a summarized inside join with sums and means?
questions.explain: Choose the fields and the statistics to calculate.

questions.prompt: Which QGIS tool is a shortcut for counting points in each polygon?
questions.explain: It adds a count field to each polygon.

questions.prompt: In ArcGIS Pro's Spatial Join tool, the destination layer is called the:
questions.explain: The join features are the source.

questions.prompt: In ArcGIS Pro's Spatial Join, checking Keep all target features gives:
choices: A left join that keeps unmatched targets
questions.explain: Unchecked, unmatched targets are dropped.

questions.prompt: In ArcGIS Pro's Spatial Join, which match option gives a simple distance join?
questions.explain: Set a distance field name to record the distance.

questions.prompt: To count crashes within 30 feet of each road in ArcGIS Pro, use:
choices: Within a distance, with a 30-foot search radius
questions.explain: Join_Count gives the number of crashes near each road.

questions.prompt: In QGIS, a count of points within a radius of each feature is done by:
choices: Buffering the features, then Join Attributes by Location (Summary)
Join Attributes by Nearest with 0 neighbors
questions.explain: The buffer is the search distance.

questions.prompt: A simple join that keeps all destination features has more rows than the destination layer. Why?
choices: A one-to-many join repeated some features
questions.explain: Check the join type: one-to-many creates a row for each match.

questions.prompt: A distance field shows values like 0.12 for cities that are many kilometers apart. What happened?
choices: The data were in a geographic CRS, so the distances are in degrees
The cities are very close together
questions.explain: Project first, then rerun.

questions.prompt: Find districts with more than 10 earthquake deaths. The best plan is:
choices: Districts as destination, a summarized inside join with the sum of deaths, then a query
Earthquakes as destination, a simple inside join
A simple distance join from districts to earthquakes
An attribute join on district name
questions.explain: Each district can contain many earthquakes.

questions.prompt: Score rivers by the population of the counties they flow through. The relationship is:
choices: Inside (intersects), one-to-many, summarized with a sum
questions.explain: Each river crosses many counties.

questions.prompt: The closest volcano to each U.S. city is a:
choices: Simple distance join, cities as destination
Summarized inside join, volcanoes as destination
Summarized distance join, cities as destination
questions.explain: Many cities can share a nearest volcano: many-to-one.

questions.prompt: Put the planning questions for a spatial join in order.
answer: Decide what one row of the output represents
questions.explain: Start from the output, then work out the join.

questions.prompt: A distance join matches Asheville to Knoxville's airport, because the source layer leaves out Asheville's own airport. This shows that:
choices: A join is only as good as the source layer
Distance joins never cross state lines
questions.explain: Always ask whether the source contains every feature that could be the answer.
